parts: A finish is a treatment given to a fabric to change its appearance, handling (touch) or performance and make it more suitable for its end use. A fabric given a finish is a finished textile. Gray goods (unfinished textiles) come directly from the loom, are dull, wrinkled and uneven, have little customer appeal and are used for rough work, backing or packaging; they are not actually gray in colour. Finishes improve appearance, give variety through dyeing and printing, improve feel, make fabric more useful, improve the draping of light fabrics and suit an end use.

By function: basic (aesthetic) finishes applied to almost all fabrics – scouring, bleaching, starching, calendering, and also dyeing and printing; functional or special finishes for a specific purpose – fire-proof, waterproof, bullet-proof, crease-resistant. By degree of performance: temporary (run off in the first wash, e.g. starching), semi-durable (last several washes, e.g. bleaching), durable (last the life of the fabric, e.g. permanent pleats, wrinkle-resistant), permanent (chemical treatment changes the fibre, e.g. waterproofing, fire-proofing). By process: chemical (wet) finishes – durable or permanent, e.g. fire-proof, crease-resistant; mechanical (dry) finishes – moisture, pressure, heat or a device, e.g. beating, brushing, calendering – temporary or semi-durable.

Scouring (cleaning): industrial washing of fabric with warm water and soap solution to remove oils, starches and waxes; it cleans the fabric and makes it more absorbent (cotton is boiled in soap solution, silk is boiled to remove gum – degumming, wool is boiled to remove grease). Bleaching: a chemical treatment to remove paleness or colour and make fibre, yarn or fabric white; hydrogen peroxide for protein fibres (silk, wool) and sodium hypochlorite for cotton; man-made fibres need none; strong bleach damages fabric. Starching (stiffening): makes fabric heavier, stiff, crisp, shiny and smooth (muslin, poplin, cambric, thin silks); loosely woven fabric starched heavily shows its weave after the first wash. Calendering: industrial ironing – the fabric passes through smooth hot rollers to remove wrinkles and give a smooth, lustrous look.

Pre-shrinking (sanforisation) prevents shrinkage after washing (labels: sanforised, anti-shrink, shrink-proof). Mercerisation: cotton is treated with sodium hydroxide to make it strong, lustrous and absorbent and to improve dye uptake (routine for cotton; sewing threads are mercerised). Parchmentisation: cotton is treated with a mild acid that partly eats away the fabric, giving permanently stiff, transparent, light organdy that needs no starch. Wash 'n' wear: cotton, linen or wool treated so that it does not wrinkle much and can be worn without or with little ironing. Dyeing gives solid colour; printing applies colour only to selected areas to make designs; the colour should be colourfast.
Dyes, stages of dyeing, decorative dyeing and printing

Natural dyes (turmeric, henna, madder, indigo from plants; tyrian purple and lac from animals; khaki from minerals) are eco-friendly but slow, difficult and expensive. Synthetic dyes (direct, basic, acid, disperse, azo, vat, reactive) are easy to use, brighter and faster but polluting and may cause allergies; azo dyes are banned. Textiles are dyed at the fibre stage (popular for man-made fibres, uniform and fast, but wastage), yarn stage (knitting yarn, threads), fabric stage (most dyeing; uniform; good for blends) and garment stage (piece dyeing; no fabric wastage but colour may be uneven near seams).

Resist (decorative) dyeing uses a resist to keep dye from selected areas. Tie and dye uses thread: marbling, binding, knotting, folding, peg tying, tritik; Patola of Gujarat is tied and dyed in the yarn before weaving, bandhani of Rajasthan in the woven fabric. Batik uses wax (beeswax and paraffin wax) as the resist, removed later. Printing methods: block, screen, roller, stencil; in block printing a wooden block with an engraved design is pressed into thick dye paste and stamped on the fabric (Sanganer, Jaipur); at home vegetables such as ladies' finger or onion can be used as blocks.
